blocks.text: The Batch API lets a caller submit a large collection of requests together as a single asynchronous job, instead of making each one as its own separate synchronous call, applying the request and response mechanics covered in earlier modules to a workload shape those modules did not address: thousands of requests with no one waiting on any single answer right away.

This topic covers the JSONL request file format, uploading a batch file and creating a job, the completion window and job status states, retrieving and matching results, handling partial per-request failures, and when batch processing is the right choice over an ordinary synchronous call.
1. Why the Batch API Exists

blocks.alt: A large collection of requests with no one waiting on an immediate answer is better submitted together as one Batch job

blocks.text: Some workloads, classifying a large archive of support tickets, generating embeddings for an entire document library, running a bulk evaluation over thousands of test cases, do not need any single response back within a second. The Batch API exists specifically for this shape of work, trading immediate responses for meaningfully lower cost and simpler large-scale request management.
2. The JSONL Request File Format

blocks.alt: A batch file is JSONL: one complete, independent request object per line

blocks.text: A batch submission is a JSONL file, one JSON object per line, no enclosing array. Each line carries a custom_id the caller assigns, the HTTP method and endpoint URL being called, exactly as covered in the earlier HTTP Methods topic, and the request body itself, exactly the same body shape used in an ordinary synchronous call to that same endpoint.

code.content:
{"custom_id": "ticket-1001", "method": "POST", "url": "/v1/chat/completions", "body": {"model": "gpt-4", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Classify this support ticket: My payment failed twice."}]}}
{"custom_id": "ticket-1002", "method": "POST", "url": "/v1/chat/completions", "body": {"model": "gpt-4", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Classify this support ticket: How do I reset my password?"}]}}

blocks.text: 3. Uploading the File and Creating the Job

blocks.alt: Uploading a JSONL file and creating a batch job from it

blocks.text: The JSONL file is uploaded first, exactly like uploading training data for fine-tuning, covered in the previous topic, receiving back a file id. That file id is then passed when creating the batch job itself, along with the target endpoint and the completion window.

code.content:
batch_file = client.files.create(file=open("tickets.jsonl", "rb"), purpose="batch")

batch_job = client.batches.create(
    input_file_id=batch_file.id,
    endpoint="/v1/chat/completions",
    completion_window="24h",
)

blocks.text: 4. The Completion Window

blocks.alt: A batch job trades an immediate response for a bounded completion window, typically twenty-four hours, at meaningfully lower cost

blocks.text: A batch job is guaranteed to finish within its stated completion window, commonly twenty-four hours, not instantly. The job can, and often does, finish well before the deadline, but nothing in the caller's own workflow should assume it completes within seconds the way a synchronous call does.
5. Job Status States

blocks.alt: A batch job moves through validating, in_progress, and finalizing toward completed, or ends in failed or expired

blocks.text: A batch job's status moves from validating, checking the uploaded file is well formed, through in_progress and finalizing, to completed. A job can also end as failed, if the submission itself was invalid, or expired, if it could not finish within the completion window.

code.content:
status = client.batches.retrieve(batch_job.id)
print(status.status)  # validating, in_progress, finalizing, completed, failed, or expired

blocks.text: 6. Retrieving and Matching Results

blocks.alt: Results are matched back to their original request using the same custom_id, not by their position in the file

blocks.text: Once completed, the job exposes an output file id. That output file is itself JSONL, one result line per submitted request, each one carrying the same custom_id the caller originally assigned, since results are not guaranteed to come back in the same order the requests were submitted.
7. Handling Partial Failures

blocks.alt: Most requests in a large batch typically succeed, while a few individual ones can fail independently, reported separately by custom_id

blocks.text: A single malformed request inside a large batch, such as an oversized prompt or an invalid parameter, does not fail the entire job. That one request's failure is instead recorded in a separate error file, keyed by its own custom_id, while every other request in the same job is processed and returned normally.

blocks.title: Always Reconcile Both Files
blocks.content: A complete batch integration checks both the output file for successes and the error file for individual failures, matching every custom_id sent back against the two together, rather than assuming a completed job means every single request inside it succeeded.

blocks.text: 8. Batch API vs Synchronous Calls

blocks.alt: Whether a human is waiting on a specific response right now is the deciding factor between synchronous calls and the Batch API

blocks.content: {"headers":["Synchronous Chat Completions","Batch API"],"rows":[["Response arrives in seconds","Response arrives within the completion window, commonly up to 24 hours"],["Full per-request pricing","Meaningfully discounted pricing, commonly around half price"],["Best for interactive, user-facing use","Best for large-scale offline workloads with no one waiting"],["Subject to ordinary rate limits per request","Governed by its own separate batch queue and limits"]]}

blocks.text: Neither approach replaces the other, an interactive chatbot still needs synchronous calls covered throughout the earlier modules, while a nightly bulk classification run is exactly the workload the Batch API exists for.
9. When Batch Processing Fits

blocks.alt: Large volume with no immediate response required is the clearest signal to use the Batch API

blocks.text: Bulk classification, bulk embedding generation, covered in an earlier module for the underlying concept and revisited concretely later in this module, offline evaluation runs, and any workload processing dozens or more requests with no immediate response required are the clearest fits for the Batch API.
Worked Example

A team needs to classify one hundred thousand archived support tickets by category overnight. Rather than making one hundred thousand synchronous calls, which would be slow, expensive, and constrained by ordinary rate limits, they build a single JSONL file with one request per ticket, each carrying its own ticket id as the custom_id, and submit it as one batch job before leaving for the day.

The next morning, the job has completed well within its twenty-four hour window. The team downloads the output file, matches every result back to its original ticket using custom_id, and separately checks the error file for the small handful of tickets whose content triggered a formatting issue, reprocessing only those individually.
Common Mistakes

items: Submitting a workload to the Batch API when a real user is actively waiting on that specific response
Building a malformed JSONL file, such as missing a custom_id or writing invalid JSON on one line
Checking only the output file and never reconciling the separate error file for individual request failures
Assuming a batch job completes within seconds rather than planning around its full completion window

blocks.text: Practice

Build a JSONL file with three requests, each classifying a different piece of customer feedback as positive, negative, or neutral, each with its own custom_id. Upload it, create a batch job against the chat completions endpoint, poll its status until completed, then retrieve and print the output file's results matched back to each original custom_id.
Key Takeaway

The Batch API applies the request and response mechanics from earlier modules to large, non-urgent workloads: requests are submitted together as a JSONL file, processed asynchronously within a completion window at meaningfully lower cost, and results are matched back by custom_id rather than by order, with individual failures reported separately so one bad request never derails an entire job.
